db Database Plugin > vs SQLite: Choosing Between Them

vs SQLite: Choosing Between Them

The db plugin and SQLite are often compared, but they do not solve the same problem. This page makes a structured comparison across five dimensions — storage model, transactions, query interface, type system, and embedding method — and lists the repository's own measured data verbatim. Every conclusion states its source; parts not covered by the repository documentation are expressly marked as background knowledge.

Source conventionThe four sources cited on this page are: sa_plugin_db/README.md (the plugin's main document), sci/docs/db_comparison.md (the 2026-06-12 comparison report), sci/docs/db_plugin_evaluation.md (an evaluation from the same period), and sci/docs/database.md (the sa-db design blueprint). Short names are used below.

The conclusion in one sentence

README.md's summary, verbatim: "SQLite remains stronger for SQL, index creation, ACID, WAL, crash recovery, compact/vacuum, and integrity checks." And the db plugin has the advantage in scan queries reusing a read handle, bulk columnar writes, and indexed ERP list/projection queries.

db_comparison.md's selection recommendations, recorded item by item:

  • Need SQL, indexes, transactions, or crash recovery: choose SQLite.
  • An SA program already has columnar data internally and you want to land small-table bulk writes or full-column updates quickly: the db plugin is faster in this benchmark.
  • Need production-grade long-term storage: SQLite is still clearly more solid.

Storage model

db plugin: columnar segment files, no B-Tree. Each table is split by column into a set of sequentially appended segment files (<table>.col<i>.<seg>.dat), the schema is expanded at compile time into a #def dictionary, and the row width is obtained by summing the column strides. database.md §0 summarizes this as “no SQL string parsing, no B-Tree (SoA columnar + direct jumps by physical row index)”; point lookups and range queries rely on a persisted “key -> row” sorted index plus binary search, rather than a paged tree.

SQLite: a mature relational storage layer. The technical-explanation section of db_comparison.md writes: "SQLite's storage layer, pager, WAL/lock mechanisms, and query execution path are far more mature; the db plugin currently has no SQL, indexes, transaction log, query optimizer, or crash recovery" (this sentence was written before indexes and transactions landed, and should now be understood as a qualitative statement about maturity rather than a capability list). That SQLite organizes tables and indexes as B-trees is database common knowledge; the repository documentation does not expand on it, so it is background only here.

The direct corollary differences between the two:

Dimensiondb pluginSQLite
In-row layoutStored continuously by column (SoA); a row is the logical splicing of same-ordinal slices of each columnOrganized by row within pages
Append writesNew data becomes a new segment, with the manifest advancing the epochPage splits and WAL appends
Whole-row readsMust splice the fragments of each column back into a fixed-width row bufferNaturally returns by row
Fetching only a few columnsAdvantage scenario: projection copies only the requested column bytesStill needs to unpack pages and read rows
Space reclamationcompact rewrites and merges segmentsVACUUM, measured about 3.6× faster
Integrity checkingverify checks schema/segment/block-level hashesintegrity_check, measured about 3.3× faster

Transactions and concurrency

This is where the gap between the two is largest, and also most easily misunderstood. The README's boundary statement, verbatim:

This is still not a replacement for SQLite-style ACID, WAL, general primary/secondary index planning, or multi-table transaction isolation.
Capabilitydb plugin (current state)SQLite
Transaction scopeSingle-table, single-writer; tx_begin/tx_commit/tx_rollback operate on an in-memory imageStandard transactions across multiple tables
Write serializationIn-process mutex + a per-table advisory write lock file <table>.write.lock, serializing on the same table across processesLock mechanisms + WAL concurrent reads and writes
Commit atomicityAtomic rename after syncing a temporary file; a crash before the manifest advances can fall back to the previous epochGuaranteed by the pager/WAL
Crash recoveryrecover scans versioned meta files to rebuild the manifest; transactions use pending/commit markers to distinguish unfinished from committedA mature crash-recovery path
Read concurrencyOpening a read handle no longer waits on the global mutation mutex; an active write transaction does not block opening a committed snapshotUnder WAL, reads and writes do not block each other
ConstraintsUnique indexes (u64/i64/compact integers/pair/blob_eq) act as real uniqueness constraints, violations returning SA_DB_ERR_CONSTRAINTA complete primary-key/foreign-key/CHECK/trigger system
Warningdb_comparison.md specifically warns: an in-process mutex “proves only that a same-process benchmark is correct; it is not equivalent to multi-process transaction isolation or ACID”. Before using the db plugin for strongly consistent writes across processes, you must evaluate this yourself.

Query interface: the SQL surface vs the read-handle API

The db plugin has no runtime SQL. Queries have two paths:

  1. The read-handle API: after opening a snapshot, call in memory sum/count/find/range/filter_rows/plan/sort/project/get_row/group_stats and other functions to compose a result. The README stresses that the plan family is "a planner building block rather than a SQL optimizer"; more complex shapes require explicitly composing these building blocks.
  2. Precompiled qmods: register SA query code as a module locked by SHA-256, and execute it with sa db register/sa db exec <hash>; the entry point must declare db_read/db_write/db_atomic_cursor grants.

SQLite provides full SQL string parsing, query planning, and execution. The cost is that every row must go through a bind/step/reset loop — db_comparison.md holds that this is exactly why the db plugin pulls ahead on bulk inserts: the benchmark passes raw bytes in column layout directly, “avoiding SQLite's per-row bind/step/reset overhead”.

Type system

db plugin: physical fixed-width primitives + logical annotations. The physical layer has only fixed-width primitive columns (I1/I8/I16/I32/I64/U8/U16/U32/U64/F32/F64/PTR/BLOB_HANDLE/V128), and business types are mapped onto those bytes through schema annotations:

#def COL_AMOUNT_CENTS_STRIDE = 8 // i64 decimal(2)
#def COL_DUE_DAY_STRIDE     = 8 // i64 date
#def COL_POSTED_AT_STRIDE   = 8 // i64 timestamp_ms
#def COL_ACTIVE_STRIDE      = 1 // u8 bool
  • Amounts = scaled i64; dates = epoch days; timestamps = epoch ms/us; booleans = normalized 0/1; nullable = a sidecar null bitmap. The decimal scale limit is 18.
  • Variable-length text is not made into a column: low-cardinality values go through dictionary IDs (1-based, 0 reserved), and general text/blobs go through a store + an 8-byte handle.
  • Float indexes reject NaN and ±Inf, because their ordering is not stable business data.
  • The schema is immutable once locked; database.md §15 expressly states “dynamic schema changes are not supported (adding a column requires a new table)”.

SQLite uses dynamic typing and storage-class affinity; the same column can store values of different types, and it supports TEXT/BLOB columns of arbitrary length. This part is general background, not covered by the repository documentation; but the engineering difference it produces is real: the db plugin requires you to settle the business-type encoding scheme when you create the table, in exchange for zero parsing overhead and a stable row width.

Embedding method and permission surface

Dimensiondb pluginSQLite
Access formThe SA plugin ABI; after installation through sap.json, used via @import "db.sal"A C library; on the SA side, called via @extern sqlite3_*
Symbol sourceabi.symbols = "db.sai", about 300 sa_db_* externsC APIs such as sqlite3_prepare/step/finalize
File permissionsOnly read/write/create/delete on $PROJECT/**Decided by the host process
Network / environment / child processesAll forbidden (net:[], env:[], spawn:false)No restriction at this layer
Build artifactszig-out/lib/libdb.so / zig-out/bin/db.dllSystem libraries such as libsqlite3.so.0

On the benchmark side there is an engineering detail worth noting: the SA standard library currently exports stubs for sqlite3_prepare/sqlite3_step/sqlite3_finalize, which would override the system SQLite symbols of the same names, so when linking the SQLite comparison program you must first rename the stubs in std with objcopy --redefine-sym (see the full command in the Benchmark section of the README). This shows that using both at once in SA takes a little linking technique.

Measured data comparison

WarningEverything below is an uncalibrated microbenchmark measurement, not a product-level promise. They come from small-sample medians on a single machine (mostly 3–7 rounds), with only two workloads, a member database and a specific ERP workflow; the 2026-06-27 set, moreover, expressly ran in the unsafe/no-sync measurement mode SA_DB_UNSAFE_NO_SYNC=1. The README itself repeatedly qualifies this with "Scope is still limited to this benchmark". Treat these numbers as a relative trend reference, not as absolute performance indicators, and do not extrapolate them to your own workload.

Member database, 50,000 rows (median of 5 rounds)

Source: the Benchmark table in README.md and the single-threaded details in db_comparison.md; the two sets of numbers agree.

Queries reusing a read handle and concurrent writes (2026-06-18, isolated roots, median of three rounds)

Operationdb pluginSQLiteFastest
serial 100× SUM (read handle)167.317 ms338.595 msdb plugin
concurrent 4×25 SUM (read handles)157.531 ms197.866 msdb plugin
concurrent insert 4×12500 (bare ingest_columns)95.736 ms108.089 msdb plugin
concurrent insert 4×12500 (coltx batch session)72.192 ms108.089 ms*db plugin

* The SQLite side has only one concurrent-transaction insert benchmark path, and cannot distinguish bare inserts from coltx. The README also points out that this round verified two behavior changes: a read handle can be opened during an active write transaction (still seeing only the committed snapshot), and coltx staging is no longer serialized by the global handle mutex. It should be noted that db_comparison.md reported a set of markedly better-looking early numbers (serial 122.111 ms, concurrent 48.385 ms, concurrent insert 55.618 ms), but at that time the three benchmark sets shared the same root, and historical artifacts and WAL/SHM side files could contaminate each other; the README explains that only after moving each benchmark to an independent root (.bench_raw/.bench_coltx/.bench_sqlite) were the reproducible values above obtained, and the earlier intermittent concurrent failures did not recur.

The README's qualification of this set must be kept in full: "Scope is still limited to this benchmark and unsafe/no-sync measurement mode; SQLite remains stronger for general SQL, mature ACID/WAL behavior, crash recovery, vacuum/compaction semantics, and broad operational tooling." It also stresses that the benchmark executable links against the installed plugin, so after rerunning the Zig build you must redo SA_PLUGIN_DEV=1 sa plugin install --dev … to be measuring the current source.

Selection reference table

Your needRecommendationBasis
Need SQL, JOINs, views, or aggregate functions to express complex reportsSQLitedb_comparison.md selection recommendation, item one
Need ACID, WAL, cross-table transaction isolation, or mature crash recoverySQLiteREADME boundary statement + summary
Need production-grade long-term storage and an operations toolchainSQLitedb_comparison.md: “SQLite is still clearly more solid”
Frequent compact/vacuum or integrity checksSQLiteBoth member-database items are more than 3× faster
Columnar data already generated inside an SA program, to be landed in bulkdb pluginbulk insert about 2.2× faster
Repeated full-table/index scans over the same batch of datadb pluginAfter reusing a read handle, both serial and concurrent SUM are faster
ERP-style list pages, child-table details, composite-key filtering, column projectiondb pluginFive indexed ERP workflow queries about 2.7–25× faster
High-frequency initialization/rebuilding of small ERP tables with dictionaries and indexesdb pluginThe 2026-06-27 set leads in every category (unsafe mode)
Fields such as amounts that need exact decimal representationBoth work, in different waysThe db plugin uses scaled i64 + a decimal(N) annotation; floats are limited to non-amount measurements

Will the gap shrink?

The README's ERP Foundation Roadmap expressly lists the next directions: expanding the fault-injection matrix, an optional WAL, richer primary-key/secondary-index shapes, multi-table transaction semantics, and asynchronous bulk flushing; the performance side is ranked after reliability — mmap snapshots, block min/max indexes, predicate pushdown, and SIMD aggregation. That is, the current multi-table isolation and WAL gaps are deliberately scheduled follow-up work, not a permanent design abandonment. Conversely, it also expressly states that it will not chase the “general SQL” direction.

Related reading: Limits, Performance, and Best Practices gives the list of limits and actionable practice recommendations; db Plugin Overview: Positioning and Architecture describes the architectural reasons behind these behavioral differences.
